n: In this lecture we shall study methods for isolating barbituric acid derivatives from physical evidence and for analysing them. The analysis is carried out by TLC screening (thin-layer chromatography), UV spectrophotometry and other physicochemical methods. The outline is as follows: isolation and purification, TLC screening, gas and high-performance liquid chromatography, and then UV, IR and mass spectra. Colour, precipitation and microcrystalloscopic reactions, as general reactions for detecting barbiturates, were covered in the previous lecture.

First, the methods of isolation from the specimen. Barbiturates are isolated from a biological specimen by the acidified alcohol or acidified water method. For some barbiturates, specific methods are used; that is, they are isolated from the biological specimen by special procedures. From biological fluids, barbiturates are isolated by extraction with organic solvents. So the choice of method depends on the type of specimen, that is, on whether it is a solid tissue or a fluid.

Urinary excretion. Of the barbital taken, 70-80% is excreted in the urine, and of phenobarbital, 15-20%. For this reason, in poisoning the patient's urine is always examined. Long-acting barbiturates are broken down little in the liver and are excreted in the urine. The short-acting hexenal and thiopental, by contrast, are rapidly broken down in the liver; they are distributed almost evenly among the internal organs. Remember: limited breakdown in the liver is characteristic only of the long-acting drugs.

Storage time and clinical picture. Different authors give different periods for the persistence of barbiturates in biological specimens, from 1.5 to 14 months. A poisoned patient sleeps for a long time, sometimes not waking for 1-2 days; breathing is stertorous and blood pressure falls. The limbs become cold, and sometimes there is nausea and vomiting. In the end, death occurs from paralysis of the respiratory and vasomotor centres.

t: Acidified water and alcohol method: 28 substances
n: The acidified water and alcohol method. The expert must test for 28 substances: 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds. The barbiturates are: barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, etaminal sodium, cyclobarbital, that is phenodorm, hexobarbital, that is evipan, and benzonal. The acidified alcohol method was proposed for isolating alkaloids by J. S. Stas in 1851. In 1856 F. Otto modified it.

Effect of pH on extraction. Non-dissociating organic acids such as barbiturates are electrically neutral in water and are poorly hydrated by it. Therefore, when mixed with an organic solvent, they are rapidly solvated and pass into the organic layer. If the pH shifts to the alkaline side, dissociation increases and extraction into the organic solvent falls. If it shifts to the acid side, the number of undissociated molecules rises and extraction increases.

t: Alkaloids and amphoteric compounds: effect of pH
n: Alkaloids and amphoteric compounds. In an acid medium, alkaloids and synthetic nitrogenous compounds form ions and remain in the water; when alkali is added, they are extracted as bases. Amphoteric compounds include morphine, apomorphine and salsoline, with an amino group and a phenol group, and ecgonine, with an amino group and a carboxyl group. Amphoteric compounds in the molecular state are extracted well by organic solvents, whereas their ions are practically not extracted. Neutral substances such as antifebrin and phenacetin are little affected by pH.

Two chloroform extracts. Whichever method is used, the forensic chemist carries out the examination with two chloroform extracts. The first contains the toxic substances extracted from the aqueous solution into an organic solvent in an acid medium. The second contains the substances that pass into the organic solvent layer in an alkaline medium. The acid extract is examined for barbiturates, neutral substances, organic acids and weakly basic alkaloids.

t: Purification of the alkaloid extract by TLC
n: Purification of the alkaloid extract by TLC. To purify the alkaline extract, for alkaloids, the system chloroform-acetone-diethylamine 50:30:2 or chloroform-acetone-ammonia 30:20:2 is used. Dragendorff's reagent is used as the visualising reagent. For the acid extract, that is, for barbiturates, the system chloroform-n-butanol-NH3 is taken in the ratio 70:40:5, and the reagent is mercury(II) sulphate with diphenylcarbazone. Other purification steps are also carried out together with isolation: filtration, protein precipitation and centrifugation.

Factors in extraction. The distribution coefficient K equals the ratio of the concentrations in the organic solvent and in water: K = Corg / Cwater. The degree of extraction is found by the formula R = (A / N) · 100 %, where A is the amount in the organic solvent and N is the total amount in water. The factors affecting extraction are: pH, the nature of the organic solvent, the number of extractions, salting-out agents, that is electrolytes, and temperature.

t: Purifying the extract: re-extraction and sublimation
n: Purifying the extract. Acid extracts are freed of foreign substances by re-extraction; organic acids and barbiturates are purified in this way. In re-extraction the pH must be exact, otherwise the substance under investigation may be lost. Dry distillation, that is sublimation, purifies substances that sublime on heating. These include barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids, and caffeine.

Electrodialysis and electrophoresis. Electrodialysis is used to isolate and purify certain substances, such as strychnine and pachycarpine. Under a direct current, alkaloid salts migrate through a semipermeable membrane towards the cathode; for analysis, the cathode liquid is extracted. Electrophoresis is chromatographic purification under the action of an electric current. In it, salts migrate towards the cathode at different rates and are separated from one another and from foreign substances.

t: Sulphonation and preliminary test on urine
n: Sulphonation and preliminary test on urine. Sulphonation is a method of isolating substances resistant to concentrated sulphuric acid, for example barbiturates, from extracts rich in fats and lipids. In the preliminary examination, to detect barbiturate poisoning provisionally, cobalt acetate is added to the urine under ammoniacal conditions or in the presence of lithium hydroxide. The result of the provisional test is supplemented by further analyses to establish the identity of the substance.

t: Effect of electrolyte, temperature and solvent on extraction
n: Effect of electrolyte, temperature and solvent on extraction. When electrolytes are added, the solubility of substances changes; as a result of salting out, the distribution coefficient and extraction increase. The salting-out effect of small-radius ions is greater than that of large-radius ions. Electrolytes are also used to break emulsions and to precipitate protein. A change in temperature alters the distribution coefficient, and the number of extractions is determined empirically.

t: Foreign substances in the extract and methods of purification
n: Foreign substances in the extract. The extract contains foreign substances such as protein, amino acids, fats and lipids, which interfere with the analysis. The methods of purification are: settling, filtration, centrifugation, precipitation and repeated extraction. Settling and filtration may cause loss of the analyte through adsorption, so centrifugation is more convenient. Proteins are precipitated with trichloroacetic, tungstic and metaphosphoric acids, by heating to 40°C, or with absolute alcohol and acetone.

Methods of protein precipitation. Proteins in an extract obtained by settling, filtration or centrifugation are precipitated with trichloroacetic, tungstic and metaphosphoric acids and certain heteropoly compounds. By heating the solution to about 40 °C, many proteins can be precipitated. Proteins also precipitate when treated with absolute ethyl or methyl alcohol or with acetone. Precipitation of proteins in a saturated salt solution, that is salting out, is also used.

t: Purification of acidic substances by re-extraction
n: Purification of acidic substances by re-extraction. Acidic substances are extracted with alkali, that is at pH 13: here the organic layer is not needed, the aqueous layer is. Then re-extraction is carried out with acid, that is at pH 1: now the substances under investigation are in the organic layer, and the aqueous layer is not needed. Remember: with this method, neutral substances and substances with weakly basic properties are lost.

t: Purification of the alkaline extract by repeated extraction
n: Purification of the alkaline extract by repeated extraction. Here the order is reversed. The residue is extracted with acid, that is at pH 1: the organic layer is not needed, the acidic aqueous layer is. Then the aqueous layer is re-extracted with alkali, that is at pH 13: the substances under investigation are in the organic layer, and the aqueous layer is not needed. With this method, substances with weakly basic properties are lost, namely purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine.

TLC screening: system and reagents. The mobile phase consists of chloroform, n-butanol and 25% ammonia solution in the ratio 70:40:5. As visualising reagents, a 0.02% solution of diphenylcarbazone in chloroform and an aqueous solution of mercury sulphate are sprayed on. Barbiturates form a blue-violet spot with a characteristic Rf value. In other words, the colour of the spot and the Rf value together serve to identify the substance.

t: TLC: purification and verification of identity
n: TLC: purification and verification of identity. To purify and detect barbiturates among substances of acidic character, a mixture of chloroform, n-butanol and 25% NH4OH in the ratio 70:40:5 is used. The visualising reagent is a 0.02% solution of diphenylcarbazone in chloroform together with an aqueous solution of mercury sulphate. Barbiturates form ink-coloured spots over various Rf ranges. The specific reactions of barbiturates are based mainly on the formation of microcrystals with various reagents.

Column and carrier gas in gas chromatography. A glass column is used in the analysis; it is packed with Chromosorb G-HP sorbent impregnated with 3% SE-30. The column length is 2 m, and the internal diameter is 2-4 mm. The mobile phase is nitrogen, at a flow rate of 45-50 ml/min.

GC: temperature and identification. The analysis is run isothermally. The column temperature is 190-200 °C, the injector temperature is 220 °C, and the detector temperature is also 220 °C. Barbiturates are identified by their retention indices and the Kováts index.

High-performance liquid chromatography. The column is 150 mm long with an internal diameter of 2.6 mm, packed with octadecyl silica gel. The mobile phase consists of 0.1 M phosphate buffer at pH 3.5 and methanol in the ratio 60:40. The detector is a UV spectrometer, with a wavelength of 216 nm. The flow rate is 2 ml/min, and the sample volume is 20 µl.

The principle of UV spectrophotometry. In the keto, that is the acid, form, barbiturates give no characteristic maximum in the UV region. At pH 9.2, that is in 0.05 M borate buffer, they give a spectral maximum in the 239-241 nm region as the monoimide. At pH 13, that is in 1.0 M alkali solution, as the diimide they give a maximum in the 254-256 nm region. Thus the position of the maximum depends on the pH of the medium.

UV characteristics of the first group of barbiturates. Allobarbital at pH 9.2 gives a maximum at 241 nm, A=460; at pH 13, at 256 nm, A=356. Amobarbital at pH 9.2: 240 nm, A=445; at pH 13: 255 nm, A=364. Barbital at pH 9.2: 239 nm, A=549; at pH 13: 254 nm, A=427. Butalbital at pH 9.2: 240 nm, A=439; at pH 13: 255 nm, A=329.

The second group. Butobarbital at pH 9.2 gives a maximum at 239 nm, A=477; at pH 13, at 254 nm, A=388. Cyclobarbital at pH 9.2: 239 nm, A=410; at pH 13: 256 nm, A=320. Pentobarbital at pH 9.2: 239 nm, A=438; at pH 13: 255 nm, A=327. As can be seen, the maxima lie very close to one another.

The third group. Phenobarbital at pH 9.2 gives a maximum at 239 nm, A=452; at pH 13, at 254 nm, A=342. Secbutabarbital at pH 9.2: 239 nm, A=428; at pH 13: 254 nm, A=354. Secobarbital at pH 9.2: 239 nm, A=393; at pH 13: 254 nm, A=330. Vinylbital, in aqueous alkali, gives a maximum at 247 nm, A=298.

Comparison by UV. Most barbiturates give a maximum at 239-241 nm at pH 9.2 and at 254-256 nm at pH 13. But the A values, that is the absorbance of a 1% solution in a 1 cm layer, differ. At pH 9.2 it is 549 for barbital, 477 for butobarbital, 460 for allobarbital and 452 for phenobarbital. It is difficult to distinguish them by the position of the maximum alone, so the A values and other methods are needed.

IR spectra of the first group, in a KBr disc. For allobarbital the absorption bands are 1687, 1315, 925, 1219, 847 and 1640 cm-1. For amobarbital: 1725, 1696, 1758, 1317, 1240 and 850 cm-1. For barbital: 1680, 1720, 1767, 1320, 1245 and 875 cm-1. For butalbital: 1690, 1720, 1740, 1310, 1290 and 1200 cm-1. This set of bands is specific to each substance.

IR spectra of the second group. Butobarbital bands: 1696, 1727, 1760, 1242, 850 and 1215 cm-1. Cyclobarbital: 1693, 1725, 1745, 1300, 1210 and 830 cm-1. Pentobarbital: 1685, 1719, 1744, 1315, 1218 and 845 cm-1. By comparing the sets of bands, the substances are distinguished from one another.

IR spectra of the third group. Phenobarbital bands: 1712, 1684, 1670, 1770, 1310 and 1300 cm-1. Secbutabarbital: 1675, 1760, 1317, 1303, 1230 and 853 cm-1. Secobarbital: 1559, 1648, 1690, 1298, 1270 and 925 cm-1. Vinylbital: 1692, 1730, 1750, 1318, 1220 and 1630 cm-1.

Mass spectra of the first group. The m/z values are given here. Allobarbital: 41, 167, 124, 39, 80, 53, 68, 141. Amobarbital: 156, 141, 157, 41, 55, 142, 98, 39. Barbital: 156, 141, 55, 155, 98, 39, 82, 43. Butalbital: 41, 167, 168, 39, 124, 97, 141, 181.
Mass spectra of the second group, m/z values. Butobarbital: 141, 156, 41, 55, 98, 39, 142, 155. Cyclobarbital: 207, 141, 81, 79, 67, 80, 41, 77. Pentobarbital: 141, 156, 43, 41, 157, 55, 39, 98.

The general scheme of analysis. In the first stage, isolation is carried out by the acidified alcohol or water method, and the acid chloroform extract is obtained. Then screening and confirmation: TLC in a mixture of chloroform, n-butanol and ammonia in the ratio 70:40:5, followed by GC and HPLC. Finally, identification: the UV spectrum at pH 9.2 and 13, and IR and mass spectra.

Conclusion. Barbiturates are isolated by the acidified alcohol or water method; in an acid medium they pass into the organic solvent. TLC screening is carried out in a mixture of chloroform, n-butanol and ammonia in the ratio 70:40:5 and gives a blue-violet spot; GC and HPLC confirm the result. In the UV spectrum, a maximum is observed at 239-241 nm at pH 9.2 and at 254-256 nm at pH 13; IR and mass spectra complete the identification.

The first group of review questions is devoted to isolation and reactions. What toxicological and narcological significance do barbituric acid derivatives have? What specific methods are used to isolate them from a biological specimen? What general reactions exist for detection; write the equation of the reaction involving a cobalt salt and ammonia. Explain the microcrystalloscopic reactions. Which barbiturates are included in the 1971 UN Convention?

The second group of review questions concerns action and spectrophotometry. Describe the grouping of barbiturates by hypnotic action and the signs that appear in poisoning. Explain the analysis of barbiturates by TLC and the principle of UV spectrophotometry. Explain the effect of the medium on the optical properties of barbiturates; how are identity and quantity determined by the UV method? What is differential spectrophotometry, and how are specific molar absorbance values calculated?
